item.title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed–Solomon Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3067
Authors: Valentina Astore, Martino Borello, Alain Couvreur
Summary: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.

item.title: One Algebra to Multiply Them All: Fast Homomorphic Linear Algebra in Every Encoding
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3066
Authors: Jonghoo Lee, Guillaume Hanrot, Seongsu Jeon
Summary: Linear algebra is a core primitive of many applications of fully homomorphic encryption, including privacy-preserving machine learning, statistical analysis, and encrypted search. Efficient homomorphic matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplications are therefore an essential tool, and have been intensely studied over the last fifteen years.
Recent work, notably by Bae et al. and Park reduces homomorphic matrix multiplication in large dimension to the multiplication of plaintext matrices, plus a number of key switchings only linear in the dimension, enabling the use of highly efficient linear algebra primitives, such as those of the BLAS library, while limiting the homomorphic cost. These results have been extended by Cheon et al. to batches of matrix multiplications in smaller dimension. In CKKS, the corresponding algorithms rely on dedicated encodings (coefficient, SinC). Using these encodings constrains integration of these algorithms into a larger computation; in practice, one has either to perform an expensive conversion or to schedule the linear algebra within bootstrapping. Alternatively, Gentry and Lee obtain reductions in the slot encoding through a different ciphertext ring.
We obtain reductions to plaintext matrix multiplication directly in the slot encoding, over the standard power-of-two CKKS ring, showing that the change of ring of Gentry and Lee is not required for this functionality. Our approach uses the cyclic algebra of the field extension $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2N})/\mathbb Q(\mathrm{i})$ to describe endomorphisms independently of the choice of coordinates. We show that choosing a basis (which identifies endomorphisms with matrices) is exactly choosing an encoding. Algorithms written once in this language cover the functionalities of the classical encodings, for single matrices and, over subfields, for batches of smaller ones. This language also makes explicit the commutation of the secret key with the matrix, which is the key step in the product of two encrypted matrices.
The resulting algorithms admit elementary descriptions, corresponding to a precise scheduling of the key switchings, which allows them to be grouped, while the algebraic framework explains their common structure across various packings.
Our framework extends to products of an encrypted $d \times d$ matrix by an encrypted $d \times c$ matrix, where it allows a baby-step giant-step strategy even though both factors are encrypted. For ring degree $N$, with $c \mid d \mid N/2$, we evaluate a batch of $N/(2d)$ such products with $O(\sqrt{dc})$ key switchings in total, without any preprocessing of the encrypted inputs. In particular, an encrypted matrix-vector product requires only $O(\sqrt{d})$ key switchings.

item.title: (Significantly) Faster Post-Quantum Public-Key PCFs for OT
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3065
Authors: Shweta Agrawal, Kaartik Bhushan, Geoffroy Couteau, Mahshid Riahinia
Summary: Public-Key Pseudorandom Correlation Functions (PK-PCFs) enable N users to locally generate and publish their public keys on a bulletin board, from which any pair of users can non-interactively compute an unbounded number of correlated strings. These outputs can then be used to significantly speed up secure computation protocols.
A line of work has focused on building efficient PK-PCFs for Oblivious Transfer (OT) in the post-quantum regime. To this end, the recent work of Agrawal, Bhushan, Couteau and Riahinia (CRYPTO 2026), henceforth ABCR, introduces a family of lattice-based PK-PCFs that can generate 500-1K OTs per second. However, a significant gap remains compared to quantum-insecure counterparts: the state-of-the-art classical (group-based) PK-PCFs for (standard) OTs reach a throughput of roughly 30K OTs per second making them nearly two orders of magnitude faster.
In this work, we significantly improve the state-of-the-art of post-quantum PK-PCFs for OTs. We provide a new construction whose security is based on roughly the same lattice-based assumptions as used by ABCR. In contrast, we achieve a much higher throughput; we implement our construction and measure a rate of 208k OTs/sec for the sender, and 189k OTs/sec for the receiver on a single thread, and 746k/709k on six threads. Our key sizes, remain in the megabytes, similar to ABCR. Concretely, sender and receiver respectively store keys of size 188MB and 66MB.
Our speedup is obtained via a new blueprint for constructing PK-PCFs from public-key algebraic homomorphic MACs (PK-aHMACs), that we introduce and instantiate. We are optimistic that our ideas will find independent applications.

item.title: Faulting the Proof: Key Recovery Attacks on MQOM, SDitH and FAEST
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3064
Authors: Mohamed Abdelmonem, Håvard Raddum
Summary: MQOM, SDitH and FAEST are three candidates in the third round of NIST’s additional call for post-quantum signature schemes. The signature in all of them is a proof of knowledge of the secret key. We study their resistance to faults during the computation of this proof and present practical key-recovery attacks on all three schemes. Our attacks exploit a common feature among them: a value that is omitted from the signature to reduce its size is still bound through a hash. We show how an attacker can use this hash to test guesses about secret key material from faulty signatures. This yields new attacks on all three schemes and corrects an earlier analysis of fault attacks on MQOM, which assumed that the omitted value is available to the attacker. We demonstrate the attacks with clock glitches on an STM32F405 microcontroller running code from the round-3 reference implementations. The validated attacks recover the full secret key of all three schemes. These results show that the proof evaluation is a practical fault target in signature schemes based on the MPC-in-the-head and VOLE-in-the-head paradigms.

item.title: Rotten CHERIs - A Comprehensive Study of Faults in CHERI RISC-V
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3063
Authors: Jan Philipp Thoma, Maja Malenko, Yan Yan, Carl Shaw
Summary: The relentless stream of exploits based on memory vulnerabilities has prompted hardware developers to engineer new solutions that prevent these vulnerabilities at a deep hardware level. One such solution is CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions), which has attracted significant interest from academia and industry. While CHERI has proven effective at mitigating memory-safety vulnerabilities under its architectural threat model, real-world environments often expose devices to advanced attack strategies. In particular, physical attackers can launch fault attacks that greatly exceed the fault model assumed during CHERI's development. Although memory and fault attacks are vastly different, the question arises whether CHERI's memory-protection guarantees hold under a fault attack model.
To address this issue, we conduct the first fault analysis of CHERI on RISC-V systems. We analyze the impact of faults on capabilities and capability management instructions. Our threat analysis reveals opportunities and limitations for attackers, showing that CHERI raises the bar for meaningful fault attacks, but does not prevent them entirely. In order to evaluate fault attacks on generic CHERI-RISC-V systems, we have developed a functional, Spike-based fault simulator. We demonstrate successful fault attacks that can still violate CHERI's memory-safety guarantees and evaluate and discuss potential countermeasures.

item.title: A One-Residual Procedure for Deriving Inverse Expressions of Shift-Invariant Transformations
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3062
Authors: Jianhua Wang, Siwei Sun, Shahram Rasoolzadeh, Ruixi Lv
Summary: We present a one-residual procedure for deriving factorized inverse expressions of a class of shift-invariant (SI) transformations. The procedure uses iterative substitution to isolate a single residual input variable and propagates the resulting recurrence along cyclic orbits. For SI transformations with a single nonlinear product term (SNPT-SI) satisfying explicit cancellation conditions, we prove a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for bijectivity. The criterion determines the bijective state sizes and directly yields the corresponding inverse expressions.
We apply these results to construct degree-$t$ SNPT-SI permutations attaining the known inverse-degree bound $D_t(n)=n-\lceil(n-1)/t\rceil$ for every $t\ge2$ and $n>t$, except when $t=2$ and $n$ is even. Fixed-parameter families also attain this bound at infinitely many state sizes. The criterion covers the four main and all 14 additional transformations studied by Liu et al. (Journal of Cryptology, 2026). For $\chi_{n,t}$, we recover known inverse expressions and characterize multiple-preimage fibers. A bounded search certifies bijective families for 69 of 378 anchored parameter sets.

item.title: On the Hardness of Decomposed Learning with Errors Problems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3061
Authors: Biswajit Mandal, Shashank Singh
Summary: This work strengthens the known hardness reduction for the decision variant of Decomposed Learning With Errors (LWE) problem and additionally presents a reduction of its search variant. The Decomposed LWE is $t$-parametrized variant of LWE, where $t$ denotes the number of decomposed blocks. In both the cases, we reduce $t$-succinct LWE problem to the Decomposed LWE. The exiting hardness reduction for decision variant relies on Gaussian noise flooding paradigm, as a result the modulus-to-noise ratio is super-polynomial of security parameter. In this work, both the reductions hold in polynomial regime for polynomial number of decompositions.

item.title: Exploring Redundant PMNS Arithmetic for Side-Channel Leakage Reduction in ML-DSA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3060
Authors: Tom Voitzwinkler, Alexandre Berzati, Andersson Calle Viera, Fangan-Yssouf Dosso, Nadia El Mrabet
Summary: Polynomial Modular Number Systems (PMNS) have been proposed as an efficient alternative to classical modular arithmetic, with applications to elliptic curve cryptography. While existing work has focused on large-prime arithmetic, lattice-based cryptography operates over small moduli, a regime in which PMNS has not yet been studied. In this work, we explore this setting and propose a tailored PMNS instantiation for the modulus of ML-DSA, whose structure enables particularly efficient modular reductions. We further leverage the intrinsic redundancy of PMNS to construct a randomized arithmetic layer that decorrelates intermediate values from secret data, thereby reducing side-channel leakage without resorting to classical masking schemes. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed countermeasure through a comprehensive side-channel analysis, combining leakage detection with machine-learning-based profiling attacks targeting the Number Theoretic Transform. Our results demonstrate that PMNS-based randomization significantly reduces first-order leakage and provides strong resistance to practical side-channel attacks. We further assess the performance overhead of the proposed approach through cycle-accurate profiling on a RISC-V CVA6 core using Verilator. The observed slowdown is comparable to standard side-channel countermeasures reported in the literature. We identify the main computational bottlenecks and discuss how existing hardware acceleration strategies could substantially reduce this overhead, making PMNS a practical candidate for side-channel-resistant embedded implementations of lattice-based cryptography.

item.title: On the NP-Completeness of Worst-Case (2,1)-Quasi-Cyclic Syndrome Decoding
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3059
Authors: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang
Summary: We study the worst-case $(2,1)$-Quasi-Cyclic Syndrome Decoding problem ($\mathsf{QCSD}_{n,w}$) over $R_n = \mathbb{F}_2[X]/(X^n - 1)$. Given explicit polynomials $h, s \in R_n$ and an integer $w \ge 0$, the problem asks whether there exist $x, y \in R_n$ satisfying $x + hy = s$ with equal block weights $|x| = |y| = w$. We prove that worst-case $\mathsf{QCSD}_{n,w}$ is NP-complete in the low-weight regime $w < \sqrt{n}$ by giving a polynomial-time reduction from 3-Dimensional Matching (3DM). We also show that the same reduction establishes the NP-completeness of the relaxed variant requiring only $|x|, |y| \le w$. Additionally, our result extends to prime block lengths and to general fixed $(a, b)$-QCSD instances.

item.title: Elligator Prime: Injective Encodings to Elliptic Curves Without Torsion Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3058
Authors: Mojtaba Fadavi, David Jao
Summary: \textit{Encoding functions} map finite-field elements to rational points on elliptic curves and are used in many cryptographic protocols. Injective encodings with efficient inversion are of particular interest, since they allow elliptic curve points to be transmitted as strings indistinguishable from uniformly random ones, as in \textit{Elligator}. However, existing injective encodings rely on rational points of small order, which excludes important families of curves, notably those of prime order. Constructing efficient injective encodings to curves of prime order has thus remained a challenging open problem for more than a decade. Classical deterministic encodings based on Ska{\l}ba's equality apply to all curves, but this equality only guarantees that some candidate abscissa is valid and does not control the fibres of the encoding.
In this paper, we introduce \emph{Elligator Prime}, which takes a new direction in the design of encoding functions by replacing Ska{\l}ba's equality with an odd-parity identity on four injective M\"obius branches, arranged as two pairs exchanged by a fixed-point-free involution. Exactly one pair then contains exactly one valid abscissa, and the sign of the resulting point identifies that pair. This yields uniform $2{:}1$ encodings whose fibres are the orbits of the involution; choosing one representative per orbit gives an injective encoding with efficient inversion, without any rational torsion point of a prescribed order. In characteristic $p>3$, it covers every curve with $j(E)\notin\{0,1728\}$, in particular every curve of prime order with $j(E)\neq0$, and the curves with $j(E)\in\{0,1728\}$ that have a nonzero rational $2$-torsion point. It also covers all ordinary elliptic curves in characteristic~$3$ and all ordinary binary elliptic curves $y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b$ with $b\neq1$, closing a gap left by earlier constructions.

item.title: Classical Key Agreement with Near-Quadratic Quantum Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3057
Authors: Samuel Bouaziz--Ermann
Summary: In 1974, Merkle proposed a key exchange protocol where the honest parties make $N$ queries to a random oracle to compute a secret key, while the best attacker needs to make $\Omega(N^2)$ queries to recover the key with constant probability. This protocol was later proved to be optimal by Barak and Mahmoody (Crypto'09). In the quantum setting, Belovs et al. (TQC'17) proved that for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a classical protocol with $O(N)$ expected honest queries, for which any quantum eavesdropper making $O(N^{1.5-\varepsilon})$ queries has vanishing key recovery probability.
In this paper, we give two families of classical key-establishment protocols in the random oracle query model. The first is a two-message protocol and the second is a three-message protocol with perfect agreement. In both cases the honest parties make $\widetilde O(N)$ classical oracle queries, whereas every constant-success quantum eavesdropper needs $\widetilde\Omega(N^2)$ quantum queries to recover the key. Our result is tight up to logarithmic factors, as the quadratic classical attack of Barak and Mahmoody applies in this setting. The construction combines two levels of hidden sum relations. In the two-message protocol, Alice samples random labels and encodes their bits using masked oracle blocks. A zero is encoded by a uniformly random block, while a one is encoded by a block containing a planted sum relation. Bob decodes a random subset of the labels and publishes their sum. Alice uses her original labels to identify this subset, which becomes their shared key.
We also give an efficient implementation with $O(N\log N)$ honest oracle queries and $O(N(\log N)^2)$ combined honest running time, for which recovering the key with constant probability requires $\Omega(N^{4/3})$ quantum queries.

item.title: Security Analysis of Homogeneous MQ-Based Post-Quantum Signature Schemes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3056
Authors: Kosuke Sakata, Tsuyoshi Takagi
Summary: The security of multivariate cryptography relies on the hardness of solving the public multivariate quadratic (MQ) systems over finite fields. For a homogeneous MQ map $P$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and a nonzero target $t$, Ostuzzi recently introduced the target quotient that removes one equation from $P(x)=t$, and then each solution $x$ of the resulting system has $P(x)=bt$ for some $b\in \mathbb{F}_q$. This implies that a preimage of $t$ can be recovered exactly when $b$ is a nonzero square. In this paper, we first compare reoptimized direct and quotient costs using scheme-specific Wiedemann XL (WXL) gate-count estimates. The comparison covers Hashimoto's method on all 19 recommended UOV, SNOVA, and QR-UOV parameter sets, and Thomae-Wolf (TW) and Furue-Nakamura-Takagi (FNT) on the 13 characteristic-two sets. With the ideal retry multiplier $1/p_0(q)$, where $p_0(q)$ is the acceptance probability for uniform $b$, nominal Hashimoto-WXL savings are 2.04-4.61, 1.81-3.20, and 0.05-2.44 bits, respectively. Over $\mathbb{F}_{256}$, Hashimoto's quotient procedure recovered preimages in 640 of 1,000 reduced-parameter random UOV trials (64.0% overall), corresponding to 640 of 642 non-oil returns (99.69%), close to $255/256$ (99.61%). Second, we establish an exact recovery law in the random UOV model with independent coefficients. Solvers may select solutions with arbitrary bias using only quotient equations and randomness independent of key generation. Averaged over keys and solver randomness, single-trial recovery probability equals $p_0(q)$ times the valid non-oil return probability. With positive return probability, the residual conditional on return is uniform exactly when oil-space returns have probability zero; otherwise zero has excess mass and nonzero values remain equiprobable. We also derive finite recovery bounds under stated geometric candidate conditions and exhaustive residual-blind search; the FNT argument uses collinear-quadruple counting.

item.title: Faster Provable Algorithm For Random Modular Subset Sum
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3055
Authors: Hyeonhak Kim, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee
Summary: We study random modular subset sum with $n$ coefficients sampled independently and uniformly modulo $Q$. The target is $t=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf x\pmod Q$, where the hidden binary vector $\mathbf x$ is fixed independently of the coefficients. We focus on the balanced density-one setting, a standard hard case with $Q=2^n$ and $\mathbf x$ of Hamming weight $n/2$. In this balanced density-one setting, Bonnetain, Bricout, Schrottenloher, and Shen (ASIACRYPT 2020) reported the best previously known classical time bound of $\widetilde O(2^{0.283n})$ bit operations, using $\widetilde O(2^{0.283n})$ bits of space, under heuristic assumptions.
We present a classical randomized algorithm for the same setting that finds a solution with overwhelming probability using at most $2^{0.2614n}$ bit operations and $2^{0.2373n}$ bits of space for sufficiently large $n$, without heuristic assumptions.

item.title: BIFOLD: Memory-Efficient Homomorphic CNN Inference over Bivariate Rings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3054
Authors: Rostin Shokri, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos
Summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables private convolutional neural network (CNN) inference, but large evaluation keys hinder practical deployment. We introduce an exponential bootstrapping method exploiting an exact trigonometric identity to achieve latency comparable to standard bootstrapping, alongside low-depth and efficient functional bootstrapping for densely packed inputs. GL's bivariate ring enables compact plaintexts and convolution fused into bootstrapping. At ring degree $N=2^{15}$, ResNet-20 inference on an RTX 5090 takes 127.8 ms, $2.19\times$ faster than RBOOT, the fastest state-of-the-art baseline implemented on the same GPU backend, with $6.1\times$ smaller evaluation keys. Seeding mask polynomials reduces keys to 0.84 GB at 140.1 ms latency, advancing practical privacy-preserving machine learning.

item.title: DEEP Revisited: Proximity Gaps up to List-Decoding Radius via Out-of-Domain Samples
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3053
Authors: Alexander Frolov, Justin Thaler, Eylon Yogev, Kai Zhe Zheng
Summary: We revisit the use of out-of-domain samples for proximity gaps, introduced in DEEP-FRI. Over sufficiently large fields, multiple samples yield proximity gaps for linear codes at any list-decodable radius below the code’s minimum distance.
For general linear codes, this extends the proximity-gap guarantee from the one-and-a-half Johnson bound to the full Johnson bound using a constant number of out-of-domain samples. With a constant fraction of agreement loss and field size q at least the blocklength, the error is $O(1/q)$, yielding roughly 20 to 30 additional bits of soundness in typical hash-based SNARK settings.
For Reed-Solomon codes, the bounds apply beyond the Johnson radius even when the list size $L$ is much larger than $2^\lambda$. When the field is sufficiently large for the target error, $O(\log L / \lambda)$ out-of-domain samples suffice to achieve error $2^{-\lambda}$.

item.title: One-Bit-per-Gate Distributed Garbling and Constant-Round Malicious MPC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3052
Authors: Hanjun Li, Huijia Lin, George Lu
Summary: Distributed garbling, introduced by Beaver, Micali, and Rogaway (BMR), lets N mutually distrustful parties jointly run the garbling algorithm: as long as one of them is honest, the resulting garbled circuit, together with its input, decoding, and authentication keys, satisfies the privacy and authenticity guarantees of the base garbling scheme, as if produced by a single trusted garbler. A long line of work has improved upon BMR, achieving malicious security against all-but-one corruptions and impressive concrete efficiency. However, these protocols all inherit the Ω(𝜆|C|) garbling size of Yao-style schemes, resulting in every garbler incurring Ω(𝜆) bits of communication per circuit gate.
We present a distributed garbling protocol in which every garbler communicates an amortized one bit per gate, assuming Ring-LWE and constant-locality PRGs. It enjoys constant round complexity and is secure against a malicious adversary corrupting all but one garbler. Moreover, for sufficiently large circuits C (relative to their depth, input / output length and the security parameter), our garbling scheme and distributed protocols have the following efficiency features: • One bit per gate. The garbled circuit is |C|(1+o (1)) bits, as is each garbler’s total communication for generating and revealing it. • Distributing the garbler is almost free. Each garbler’s communication and computation exceed those of a single trusted garbler by only an additive o(|C|) term. • An efficient base scheme. Our one-bit-per-gate garbling scheme is itself lightweight: garbling is dominated by O(1) operations in the Ring-LWE ring per gate, plus a global computation dependent only on the depth, input, and output lengths of the circuit.
Our protocol immediately gives constant-round maliciously secure MPC for any number of parties with per-party communication of one bit per gate, and removes the single point of failure in other applications of garbling, such as enabling distributed generation of ciphertexts in one-key functional encryption or distributed preprocessing in outsourced computation.
Previously, for more than two parties, distributed succinct garbling was known only as a feasibility result via running generic MPC on succinct-time RAM garbling schemes, which rely on iO or similarly heavyweight tools and are prohibitively expensive computationally. Since other (more efficient) succinct garbling schemes are only succinct in size rather than time, running said schemes under generic MPC yields communication |C|poly(𝜆) as overhead from the latter.

item.title: Computational Bernoulli Smoothing and Worst-Case Errors in LPN Reductions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3051
Authors: Nathan Geier, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan
Summary: Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) is a central problem in modern post-quantum cryptography. Recently, Aggarwal et al. (TCC 2026) proposed a new approach toward establishing worst-case foundations for the hardness of LPN in the low-noise regime. Their reduction turns an average-case LPN solver into two algorithms such that, for every (worst-case) linear code, either one decodes noisy codewords of that code or the other distinguishes noisy codewords of its dual from uniform. Their main technique, computational code smoothing, relaxes a requirement of earlier reductions: noisy dual codewords need only be computationally pseudorandom, rather than statistically close to uniform.
However, their result requires random Bernoulli errors for the decoding alternative (so only the code is worst case) and fixed-weight noise for the dual distinguishing alternative (rather than the more common Bernoulli noise). We remove both of these restrictions using a new analytical technique.
As our main technical tool, we establish a computational Bernoulli perturbation bound for finite groups, which may be of independent interest. We show that if multiplying a random group element from some distribution $D$ by a fixed element with probability $\beta<1/2$ produces an $\varepsilon$-pseudorandom distribution, then $D$ itself is $\varepsilon/(1-2\beta)$-pseudorandom. This bound is tight. As a result, for Bernoulli-weighted sums in abelian groups, we show that revealing any $k$ coefficients increases the distinguishing advantage by at most a factor of $(1-2\beta)^{-k}$. This can be viewed as the computational generalization of the Bernoulli smoothing technique of Yu and Zhang (CRYPTO 2021).

item.title: MechCrypto: Agent-Assisted Cryptanalysis of the First-Round NGCC Candidates
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3050
Authors: Zhengyang Wang, Yichuan Cao, Kunyu Wu, Hongbo Li, Xiao-Shan Gao
Summary: Evaluating large batches of cryptographic submissions demands sustained scrutiny across mathematical design, security proofs, concrete parameters, and implementation code. Although large language model (LLM) agents have begun uncovering genuine flaws in public competitions, general-purpose coding agents remain brittle in cryptanalysis: they routinely miss implicit security notions and community conventions, drift outside the intended parameter or threat-model scope, and lose consistency across coupled proofs, complexity estimates, code, and prior literature. We present MechCrypto, a cryptanalytic research agent built on a persistent graph-structured framework. MechCrypto combines explicit task contracts, typed cross-artifact provenance, adaptively loaded cryptographic knowledge packs, and an independent verification gate that checks both evidential soundness and contract coverage before releasing reproducible artifacts. We evaluate MechCrypto blind on all 119 first-round candidates of the Next-generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms (NGCC) program (34 digital signatures, 41 key encapsulation mechanisms, 9 key exchange protocols, and 35 hash functions) without access to existing NGCC attack reports. The campaign with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 produces 115 comparable principal results, including 23 Critical findings. Against the 24 November 2026 public-results snapshot, MechCrypto achieves higher candidate-level severity on five submissions and identifies 57 principal findings whose underlying mechanisms have no matching public entry. Notably, for MEGASCON, MechCrypto derives an explicit, zero-search collision in the AVX-512 S-box compiled from Listing~3 of the specification, raising the candidate from the public tracker's High rating to Critical. Reports, proofs, code, and campaign data are available at https://github.com/MechMath/NGCC-results.

item.title: Resource-Aware Deployment of NIST Additional PQC Signatures on Automotive ECUs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3049
Authors: Dominik Marchsreiter, Georg Carle
Summary: The transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is vital for securing next-generation automotive architectures. However, deploying candidate algorithms from the NIST Round 3 Additional PQC Signature track onto automotive ECUs, such as those based on the Infineon AURIX TC4 (TriCore v1.8 architecture), is severely obstructed by stringent hardware constraints. Standard reference implementations incur excessive stack and heap memory demands that exceed the limited capacity of the core's Data Scratchpad RAM (DSPR), triggering memory overflows and fundamentally jeopardizing real-time predictability and system dependability. To resolve this challenge, this paper presents a systematic software-level memory optimization approach framed as a resource-aware design-space exploration across the NIST Round 3 additional signature candidates. We strategically tailor memory layouts and buffer lifetimes to strictly satisfy the hard DSPR boundaries of the AURIX TC4 core, targeting a core RAM budget of at most 171.4\,kB (with up to 139.4\,kB stack and 32\,kB heap) while offloading non-sensitive artifacts to global RAM, while preserving execution efficiency and worst-case timing behavior for time-critical automotive tasks. We evaluate our optimized implementations of MQOM, SDitH, MAYO, and QR-UOV on real automotive hardware, providing comprehensive empirical benchmarks of execution cycle counts and memory footprints against baseline implementations of ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. Our results identify MAYO-3 with our memory optimizations (MAYO-3-memopt) as the best-performing candidate overall, achieving keygen, sign, and verify times of 10.4\,ms, 24.9\,ms, and 11.5\,ms, respectively, while candidates such as SLH-DSA and SDitH remain unsuitable for on-device signing due to prohibitive execution latency, despite fitting comfortably within the memory budget. Our findings show that not all NIST Round 3 additional signature candidates are equally suited to such constrained environments, but that with targeted memory optimization, at least some can be predictably integrated into memory-constrained automotive controllers without compromising real-time guarantees or system reliability.

item.title: Which Pairs Belong Together? An Optimization Approach to Pair Selection in $F_4$
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3048
Authors: Noah Peroš, Alessandro Amadori, Jins de Jong, Pınar Kılıçer
Summary: The security of multivariate public key cryptosystems (MPKC) relies in part on the hardness of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem, which consists in finding a solution to a system of quadratic equations over a finite field. One of the main approaches to solving such systems is to compute a Gröbner basis, which is often done with Faugère's $F_4$ algorithm. In each iteration, $F_4$ selects a set of critical pairs to reduce, and the selection strategy strongly affects its performance. The standard approach, the normal strategy, selects pairs by degree alone. In this work, we introduce two features of critical pairs, novelty and column growth, and use them to formulate pair selection as a weighted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. By studying different weightings, we find that penalizing novel pairs and strongly weighting column growth reduces the computation time of $F_4$, excluding the cost of selection, by a median factor of about 1.5, at the cost of a far more expensive selection step. Based on these findings, we design the coverage strategy that keeps the two features but replaces the optimization by a sequential rule with a budget derived from the expected number of new head terms. Experiments on weakly overdetermined MQ instances over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$ with 11 to 16 equations show that the coverage strategy reduces the total computation time, including selection, by 35% to 67% compared to the normal strategy, without additional memory, and that this improvement grows with the size of the system.

item.title: Forging Encrypted Linear Checksums in Verifiable FHE: A Cryptanalysis of DataSeal
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3047
Authors: Jiseok Bang, Seungkwang Lee
Summary: DataSeal (IEEE S&P 2025) gives an FHE evaluator encrypted secret linear checksums. We study whether it can use them to make an incorrect output pass verification. Each of DataSeal's two published matrix checks separately admits substitution of a different public function without ciphertext multiplication. Even when both checks are enforced, two independent authenticated input columns yield a nonzero checksum-preserving error with probability $1-q^{-2}$ over a uniform key, provided the forged circuit decrypts correctly. This attack has multiplication depth one when the input columns are encrypted; public basis columns permit depth-zero attacks. We then analyze a natural repair: adding independent checksum rows. For $t\ge2$ rows, we bound the success probability of fixed-coefficient affine attacks and give nearly matching public-vector constructions of order $q^{-(t-1)}$. Extra rows reduce success in this class, but exposing encrypted tags costs approximately one row of protection relative to blind rank-one errors. With $t+1$ independent authenticated vectors, a cofactor attack succeeds with probability at least $1-1/(q(q-1))$ if its circuit decrypts. Its depth is $\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil$ for encrypted vectors. For public vectors, depth $\lceil\log_2t\rceil$ is necessary and sufficient for universal polynomial cancellation in our fixed-coefficient model and field range; partial cofactors characterize intermediate attacks. Independent SEAL/BGV runs execute the DataSeal forgeries and selected multi-row circuits, including a depth-two three-row cofactor. A parameter study finds settings where honest workloads decrypt but an added depth-one forgery fails, while depth-zero public-basis forgeries still execute. Independent MNIST models show forgeries that pass verification and change predictions. These experiments measure feasibility for our layouts and modulus chains; the authors' unpublished implementation and settings remain untested.

item.title: Stateful LLM Guardrails without Surveillance via Anonymous Risk Token
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3046
Authors: Anirban Chakrabarti, Stefan Dziembowski, Arup Mondal
Summary: Safety guardrails for large language models (LLMs) judge each message on its own, yet multi-turn jailbreaks spread a harmful request over messages that each look benign. To catch them, a guardrail must remember the user's earlier messages. If the provider, who hosts and runs the model, keeps this memory, it holds a permanent record of every user, almost all of whom are innocent, along with how suspicious the guardrail judged each of their private queries. One data breach, court order, or change of policy could expose this record. If the user keeps the memory instead, a malicious user can roll it back or reset it. We therefore ask whether a guardrail can remember what it needs for safety without profiling its users.
We first show that a guardrail needs far less memory than a full transcript: two numbers per user suffice. Using the classifier Llama Guard 3 on about 10,000 public conversations from automated multi-turn attacks, human red-teaming, and real users, we keep a fast and a slow running average of each user's scores; when the fast one rises above the slow one, the user's messages are becoming more harmful. At a 5% false-alarm rate, the two averages detect 34% of escalating attacks, against 25% for judging each message on its own. Kept across conversations, they cannot be evaded by splitting an attack over several conversations, unlike memory that restarts with each one. Against red-team attacks, which are often harmful from the first message, memory adds little.
To keep these averages without a profile, we introduce and design a new cryptographic primitive, anonymous risk tokens (ART), in which the user holds its own averages. For each message, the provider learns only a coarse risk level (e.g., low or high) and cannot link it to the user's earlier conversations; the user cannot lower, roll back, or copy its averages, or reset them without forfeiting a prepaid balance. We formalize the security of ART and give a provably secure construction from Pointcheval-Sanders (PS) blind signatures and zero-knowledge arguments. The price is some loss of detection within a single conversation, because the averages must start from a public value. We implement a prototype of ART in Rust and evaluate it: each message takes each party about 0.4s on one laptop core, and the user uploads 90KB, regardless of the history length.

item.title: Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption, Revisited
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3045
Authors: Dennis Faut, Chuanwei Lin, Tapas Pal, Andy Rupp
Summary: Anamorphic encryption lets ordinary ciphertexts carry an additional message whose presence remains hidden even when the ordinary decryption key is exposed. We revisit this goal in the broadcast setting studied by Do et al. (EUROCRYPT 2025) and give a distinguishing attack against their Dual-Regev construction. Given one encryption query and the ordinary secret key, an adversary distinguishes ordinary and anamorphic ciphertexts with non-negligible advantage by testing the decryption residual before rounding.
We construct an anamorphic broadcast channel for the Dual-Regev public key encryption scheme that delivers a common $L$-bit message to a fixed group in one ordinary ciphertext. Using only public information from the ordinary setup, the sender samples encryption randomness correlated with the recipients' anamorphic public keys, leaving ordinary decryption and its residual distribution unchanged. We prove anamorphic security and anamorphic-message privacy with the ordinary secret key exposed, and joint message privacy for both messages when that key is not exposed. These guarantees follow from LWE in the standard model. We instantiate the channel in the batched laconic encryption core of registration-based encryption (Klooß et al., S&P 2026) and in the encryption layer of Epoque (Boyen et al., EuroS&P 2021). These instantiations illustrate the broader applicability of our embedding technique to schemes built on Dual-Regev encryption.
We implement the basic construction and both applications in Rust and demonstrate ordinary and anamorphic message recovery from the same ciphertext using the corresponding decryption keys. With the same parameters for the ordinary layer, both modes have comparable encryption times after a one-time preprocessing of the group members' anamorphic public keys.

item.title: Quorus 2.0: Practical and Scalable Threshold Signature Scheme for NIST-Standardized ML-DSA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3044
Authors: Alexander Bienstock, Leo de Castro, Antigoni Polychroniadou, Akash Shah, Akira Takahashi
Summary: ML-DSA is a widely adopted post-quantum signature algorithm, standardized by NIST as FIPS 204. A threshold signature scheme for ML-DSA lets a group of signers, none of whom holds the key, produce signatures that verify under the unmodified, standardized verification. Existing approaches are limited in different ways: they are bound to at most 6 parties, require threshold fully homomorphic encryption, or scale to many parties but spend tens of online rounds and a heavy preprocessing phase involving mixed arithmetic--Boolean computation. Moreover, to avoid evaluating a cryptographic hash function inside multi-party computation (MPC), they reveal the transcripts of rejected signing attempts. To make these transcripts simulatable, they either modify the underlying ML-DSA signing algorithm by adding noise, or rely on a computational assumption beyond those underlying ML-DSA.
We first prove that rejected ML-DSA transcripts can be simulated statistically, with no added noise and no additional assumption, so that output signatures follow exactly the standardized distribution. Building on this result, we construct an efficient threshold protocol using only arithmetic modulo ML-DSA's native modulus $q$ that, for the first time, simultaneously (i) scales to any number of parties $n$ with $t<n/2$ malicious corruptions, (ii) has only 4 online signing rounds and $3.3\times$ less online communication than the round-optimized instantiation of the closest previous protocol, Quorus (USENIX Security~'26), which takes 16 rounds, (iii) has a far lighter preprocessing phase, with fewer than 20 rounds against 81 to 108 for Quorus, and over an order of magnitude less communication as the number of parties grows, and (iv) avoids any extra primitive or assumption beyond those underlying ML-DSA. In a wide-area deployment with tens of parties spread over different continents worldwide, the online phase of our protocol completes in under a second.

item.title: TB-IOPP: Repair-Group-Local IOPs of Proximity for Tamo–Barg Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3043
Authors: Seunghyun Cho, Saehoon Jung, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: Reed-Solomon IOPPs underpin transparent succinct arguments but inherently lack small-locality symbol repair: by the MDS barrier, reconstructing missing queries requires global recovery, creating a fundamental structural mismatch in distributed, authenticated, and data-availability settings. We introduce TB-IOPP, the first repair-group-local IOP of proximity for locally recoverable Tamo-Barg codes. TB-IOPP delegates global proximity testing to an arbitrary Reed-Solomon backend via full-rank matrix folding while strictly confining every query to the committed original oracle within a fiber, an individual local repair group.
The central technical challenge is cross-fiber stitching, where locally valid repair groups fail to combine into a globally consistent codeword. We resolve this by proving a robust anti-stitching theorem that bounds distance to the code in the fiber metric, showing that our original-oracle query complexity is optimal up to a constant factor in the ideal-IOPP model. Furthermore, we establish round-by-round knowledge soundness assuming only round-by-round soundness and efficient witness decoding of the backend, and compile the protocol under BCS into a non-interactive argument whose extraction guarantee binds directly to the published commitment. Finally, we establish a correlated-agreement theorem directly in the fiber metric to enable batched verification, and construct a splicing-resistant repairable proximity certificate tailored for authenticated distributed storage.

item.title: End-to-End Framework for Maliciously Secure Threshold Homomorphic Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3042
Authors: Intak Hwang, Jinyeong Seo
Summary: We study $t$-out-of-$n$ threshold homomorphic encryption (ThHE) and its instantiation as a maliciously secure multiparty computation (MPC) protocol. We observe that recent ThHE constructions often focus on individual phases, such as distributed key generation or distributed decryption, rather than providing an end-to-end protocol with a comprehensive security analysis. Furthermore, most existing constructions either consider only passive security or address malicious security at a theoretical level, without providing concrete instantiations or evaluating the associated overhead. Consequently, there remains a lack of practical ThHE constructions that can serve as a drop-in replacement for an MPC functionality while achieving malicious security without relying on additional ideal functionalities for key generation or secure decryption, such as a trusted dealer or an external MPC functionality.
In this work, we address these limitations by constructing a ThHE scheme and its associated secure computation protocol in an end-to-end manner, covering all phases from distributed key generation to distributed decryption. We provide a comprehensive security analysis of the resulting protocol against malicious adversaries within the universal composability framework. Furthermore, we quantify the concrete overhead of achieving malicious security by instantiating and benchmarking all the required zero-knowledge arguments of knowledge for verifying the well-formedness of cryptographic materials generated throughout the protocol execution. Our benchmarks demonstrate the practicality of our proof system instantiations, with proving times typically around 5 seconds per phase for a small parameter setting with ring degree $2^{13}$ and a 200-bit ciphertext modulus, and around one minute per phase even for a large parameter setting with ring degree $2^{15}$ and an 800-bit ciphertext modulus, using only a single thread. Furthermore, the resulting proof sizes remain practical, reaching at most 10 MiB per phase, while the public key materials can be as large as 90 MiB.

item.title: Internal Differential Collision Attacks against Round-Reduced SHA-3
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3041
Authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Chengan Hou, Meicheng Liu
Summary: The \sc{Keccak} hash function was selected by NIST as the winner of the \texttt{SHA-3} competition in 2012 and was adopted as the \texttt{SHA-3} hash standard of NIST in 2015. This paper focuses on internal differential collision attacks on round-reduced \texttt{SHA-3} and various \sc{Keccak} variants. Inspired by the work of Dinur, Dunkelman and Shamir in 2013, we propose an improved variant of internal differential cryptanalysis as well as a new target internal difference algorithm by probabilistic linearization. More exactly, we improve the internal differential cryptanalysis by abstracting new concepts such as \emph{differential transition conditions} and \emph{differential transition system}, and propose conditional internal differentials to reduce the complexity of the first two rounds. In terms of Sbox linearization, we proposed \emph{full Sbox linearization} and \emph{probabilistic Sbox linearization} techniques for internal differentials. We also exploit new strategies for optimizing the internal differential characteristic. Furthermore, we determine the expected size of collision subsets in internal differentials, by analyzing the collision probability of the digests rather than the intermediate states input to the last nonlinear layer. These techniques enhance the analysis of internal differentials, leading to the best theoretical collision attacks on nine \sc{Keccak} instances, including six round-reduced instances of \texttt{SHA-3} and three instances of \sc{Keccak} contest. Specifically, the number of attacked rounds is extended to 5 from 4 for \texttt{SHA3-384}, and the attacks on 4-, 5- and 6-round \texttt{SHAKE256} are the first collision attacks on reduced \texttt{SHAKE256}. We also present the best collision attacks for 4-round \texttt{SHA3-512} and 6-round \texttt{SHAKE128}. For the \sc{Keccak} contest, we propose theoretical collision attacks on up to 6 rounds, and successfully reduce the complexity of one previously unbroken instance to $2^{53}$.

item.title: Anamorphism Beyond One-To-One Messaging: PKE with Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3040
Authors: Xuan Thanh Do, Gaspard Meunier, Giuseppe Persiano, Duong Hieu Phan, Moti Yung
Summary: To date, Anamorphic Cryptography [EC22] has been developed to support the addition of an anamorphic plaintext message to a ciphertext carrying a regular message. The anamorphic message remains hidden even in the presence of a strong adversary that possesses the receiver’s key and/or determined the sent regular message. In this paper, we expand one-to-one encrypted anamorphic communication to one-to-many anamorphism, naturally assuming communication over a broadcast channel. What we show is that using a previously designed public-key encryption scheme, two things can happen: First, the receiver of an added hidden message may be a party different from the actual receiver (i.e., a shadow party) who has initially collaborated with the sender. Secondly, and perhaps more surprisingly, the receiving party need not be a singleton, and can be a number of different shadow (i.e., anonymous) groups, each receiving a different anamorphic message, where all these messages are extracted from one single-receiver ciphertext. The idea of having multiple hidden channels to different shadow groups is highly handy if, for example, the anamorphic messages are warnings with operational instructions, sent to the groups, and will be received by (at least one member of) a group even if the adversary is able to temporarily cut off all but one member of a channel. More specifically, • First, we motivate and formalize the notion of Public-Key Encryption with an Anamorphic Broadcast Mode, starting with the secret-key setting, where the sender and the shadow receivers share secret key material. • We then present, as an initial result of an independent interest, the first lattice-based construction of Anonymous Multi-Channel Broadcast Encryption. It is important to note here that all Multi-Channel Broadcast schemes to date are in the pairing-based setting (and are, thus, insecure against quantum adversaries). • We then show how to transform a strong form of anonymity (where the ciphertext also hides the number of channels) into a system with anamorphism in the multi-channel broadcast setting for the well-known Dual Regev Public-Key Encryption scheme. The resulting anamorphic ciphertext carries the sender’s chosen message and stays indistinguishable from a regular Dual Regev encryption of it even to an adversary holding the receiver’s secret key. • Finally, we remove the shared secret key and obtain a public-key anamorphic broadcast mode, in which the shadow receivers are addressed by their identities. To this end we build an identity-based anonymous multi-channel broadcast scheme whose public parameters are derived from the regular Dual Regev public key, and prove, in the random oracle model under the k-LWE assumption, that it endows Dual Regev with a public-key anamorphic broadcast mode: anamorphic ciphertexts are indistinguishable from regular Dual Regev ciphertexts, and, even when the dictator coerces some shadow receivers into surrendering their keys, it learns only the anamorphic bits addressed to those very receivers, and nothing about the remaining (uncoerced) receivers, neither their identities nor the messages delivered to them.

item.title: When Verification Leaks: Breaking and Repairing Verifiable PIR with Small Client Storage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3039
Authors: Ruida Wang, Xinxuan Zhang, Zirui Wang, Yijian Liu, Zhihao Li, Yi Deng, Xianhui Lu
Summary: Verifiable private information retrieval (vPIR) lets a client retrieve a database entry privately and check the server's answer. Efficient designs such as VeriSimplePIR require clients to retain a large hint: preprocessed database information needed to recover answers. Rathee, Lee, and Popa (IEEE S&P 2026) reduce this storage by using homomorphic encryption to delegate the computations involving the hint to the server. They argue that the client's acceptance or rejection of a respon se reveals no query information.
We refute this claim with two selective-failure attacks. A malicious server can modify an encrypted result so that, after decryption, the client's correctness check tests a guess about the query. Our attacks make acceptance more likely when the query matches a chosen position or falls within a chosen set. For a single-position test under the original parameters, the client accepts with probability about 6% when the guess is correct and negligible probability otherwise.
Our repair requires the server to prove that the returned ciphertext is the output of the prescribed computation. The client verifies this proof before decryption, so it rejects manipulated ciphertexts without testing their decrypted contents. We exploit the linear structure of the delegated computation to construct a compact proof checked against a short commitment to the hint. The resulting vPIR scheme provides query privacy and answer correctness against a malicious server without requiring the client to retain the large hint.

item.title: Beyond the Input-Length Barrier: AND and OT Complexity of Two-Party Computation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3038
Authors: Divesh Aggarwal, Rishav Gupta, Ananta Mukherjee, Hai H. Nguyen, Maciej Obremski
Summary: A natural quantitative question in secure two-party computation is how many calls to a complete primitive (AND, Oblivious Transfer) are necessary to securely compute a given function. Beimel and Malkin (2004) initiated a systematic study of this question for one-sided AND in perfect information-theoretically secure model against semi-honest adversaries. They gave lower bounds of $n$, the per party input length, for functions satisfying explicit combinatorial characterizations. The secure zero-communication reduction framework of Narayanan, Prabhakaran, and Prabhakaran (2020) recovered this input-length frontier by a different route. Nevertheless, unconditional lower bounds for both AND, OT beyond the per party input length for deterministic Boolean functions have remained elusive, even existentially. Our first result gives explicit AND lower bounds beyond the input length. For Inner Product, equality and Hamming proximity of $n$ bit strings, we prove lower bounds of \(1.29n+\Omega(\log n)\) AND calls. We then consider OT and show almost every Boolean function on two \(n\)-bit inputs requires \(1.26n-O(\log n)\) OT calls. For Inner Product we also improve the classical \(2n\) AND upper bound, giving a perfectly secure randomized protocol using \(1.71n+o(n)\) AND calls. The combinatorial constructions underlying this protocol may be of independent interest. Finally, we revisit the role of private randomness. We prove a general derandomization theorem showing that, near the natural counting limit, randomized protocols can be derandomized in a fully parallel way without increasing the number of AND calls. This settles the 2 and 3 AND call derandomization cases left open by Beimel and Malkin and, together with their 4 call separation, identifies 4 as the first level at which randomness helps.

item.title: LUTune: Automated Lookup Table Optimization for Efficient TFHE-Based ML Inference
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3037
Authors: Rostin Shokri, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos
Summary: TFHE evaluates quantized activation functions by programmable bootstrapping (PBS) using lookup tables (LUTs). The input precision of a LUT and the noise tolerance of its consumers affect PBS latency and evaluation-key size. LUTune rewrites activation LUTs using the outputs permitted by Concrete ML's approximate rounding rule. It folds LUTs to reduce their input precision and decomposes plaintext weights into signed digits to reduce the output-noise variance predicted for dense layers. LUTune checks the circuit failure bound under Concrete's noise model at the selected parameters. On VGG6 it achieves a $5.2\times$ speedup and a $17.2\times$ reduction in evaluation-key size relative to the lowest-latency Concrete ML configuration, using the same frozen weights and quantizers.

item.title: Dovetail: Group-Action Adaptor Signatures via a Heterogeneous Two-Block Construction
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3036
Authors: Kexiang Xiong, Gang Tang, Jie Chen, Debiao He
Summary: Adaptor signatures bind the adaptation of a pre-signature into a valid signature to the disclosure of a witness, enabling atomic swaps, payment channels, and scriptless scripts. However, existing group-action constructions face key limitations: O-IAS requires commutative actions with costly zero-knowledge proofs, Fast ORCAS incurs prohibitive communication on large group elements, and GATOR couples soundness amplification with pre-signing search cost.
We present Dovetail, a group-action adaptor signature scheme built from a heterogeneous two-block construction over multiple public keys. By pairing a large non-cheating block with a small cheating block, Dovetail decouples soundness amplification from pre-signing search cost: the pre-signer fixes both commitments, searches over nonces until the challenge hits a target support, and uses its secret key to adjust the selected responses to the challenged public keys while preserving the ordinary signature format. Following Gerhart et al.\ (EUROCRYPT 2024), we prove Dovetail secure in the classical random oracle model under the Multiple Group Action Inverse Problem ($\mathsf{mGAIP}$).
Benchmarks across CSI-FiSh, LESS, MEDS, and ALTEQ at the $128$-bit security level confirm these gains. On actions with large group elements, Dovetail outperforms both GATOR and Fast ORCAS in pre-signature size and pre-signing time, generating $15.39$ kB pre-signatures in $16.25$ ms on LESS ($s=32$, $4.6\times$ faster than Fast ORCAS) and $14.29$ kB pre-signatures in $15.20$ ms on ALTEQ ($s=64$, $121.7\times$ faster than GATOR). On compact-element actions such as CSI-FiSh ($s=4$), it produces $1.32$ kB pre-signatures in $2.49$ s, outperforming both GATOR and O-IAS.

item.title: ClearWater: A Zero-Knowledge Local-Context Hardware IP Watermarking Framework
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3035
Authors: Sakib Anwar Rieyan, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos
Summary: ClearWater embeds hardware IP watermarks during standard-cell placement in LLM-assisted flows and verifies detection without revealing the owner's key. Bounded fan-in contexts identify carrier pairs, and keyed Poseidon2 determines their relative placement order. A Groth16 proof verifies agreement over an externally audited carrier table. In our testbench, routed AES, SHA-256, and ChaCha layouts retained every registered mark with no measured cell-area growth. Copied fragments retained matching bits even when too few survived to support a detection claim. For AES, verification took 16 milliseconds. The public carrier table dominated communication, while timing impact varied across designs.

item.title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3034
Authors: Kelsey A. Jackson, Carl A. Miller
Summary: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.

item.title: FLoRA: LoRA Fine-Tuning for Language Models under Fully Homomorphic Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3033
Authors: Omar Ahmed, Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos
Summary: Deploying and fine-tuning Language Models (LMs) on cloud infrastructure introduces privacy risks when handling sensitive prompts and proprietary datasets. While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces fine-tuning overhead, it requires processing data in plaintext, exposing sensitive data to curious cloud providers. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce FLoRA, a privacy-preserving framework for encrypted LM fine-tuning and inference via Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). FLoRA allows training low-rank adapters and performing inference entirely on encrypted data, guaranteeing data confidentiality against untrusted environments. We evaluate FLoRA by fine-tuning the SmolLM2-360M model on the SST-2 dataset, demonstrating stable performance and efficiency for privacy-preserving LM adaptation.

item.title: Constant-Size Identity-Based Linkable Ring Signatures from Standard Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3032
Authors: Zhi Zhang, Jie Chen, Debiao He
Summary: In this work, we propose an identity-based linkable ring signature (IB-LRS) scheme that achieves constant-size signatures and is provably secure in the standard model under standard assumptions. All previous IB-LRS schemes are only proven secure in the random oracle model (ROM), and those achieving constant-size signatures additionally rely on non-standard assumptions. In contrast, our scheme removes both limitations simultaneously. To do this, we build our IB-LRS scheme from a constant-size hierarchical identity-based encryption (HIBE) scheme. First, we adapt this HIBE to a matrix-based dual-system framework to replace its non-standard assumptions with standard assumptions. Then, we use the ``all-but-one'' technique to aggregate all ring identities and get constant-size ring signatures. Finally, to support linkability, we add a separate matrix to bind each user's tracking key to the ring signature. Moreover, our scheme provides unconditional anonymity, and we prove its unforgeability, linkability, and non-slanderability under the Matrix Decisional Diffie-Hellman (MDDH) assumption.

item.title: (Almost) Tight Bounds for Pairing-Based SNARGs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3031
Authors: Gal Arnon, Eylon Yogev
Summary: We construct a publicly verifiable succinct non-interactive argument (SNARG) for NP in the asymmetric bilinear generic group and random oracle models. At $\lambda$ bits of security, a proof consists of one $\mathbb{G}_1$ element and $\lambda+o(\lambda)$ additional bits. Assuming exponentially secure pseudorandom generators, we show that the additional bit string cannot have length $o(\lambda)$ under natural restrictions on setup and verification. The lower bound applies to schemes with exponentially small completeness and soundness errors, where soundness holds against subexponential adversaries.
Our construction uses a variant of the KZG polynomial commitment scheme that may be of independent interest. The commitment is the hash of a target group element, and an opening proof still consists of one $\mathbb{G}_1$ element. Given the opening proof and the claimed evaluation, the verifier reconstructs the target group element with one pairing and checks its hash against the commitment, saving one pairing over standard KZG verification.

item.title: Unmasking Glitches: Why Secure Hardware Gadgets Still Leak
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3030
Authors: Dev M. Mehta, Mehmet A. Cetin, Domenic Forte, Shahin Tajik, Fatemeh Ganji
Summary: Probing-based security notions underpin the design and verification of masked hardware. Glitch-aware extensions, such as the robust probing model, provide strong guarantees within their abstraction and enable systematic gadget constructions and automated verification. Yet these guarantees do not preclude physically observable leakage: prior work shows that temperature or voltage manipulations can still induce leakage, often blamed on transient glitches without a clear root cause. To clarify, we perform a gate-level evaluation of three representative masked AND gadgets, namely HPC2, HPC3, and COMAR, under timing perturbations induced by input transitions, clock skew, and temperature variation. Our results show that these seemingly different factors share a common mechanism: they create timing differences in signal arrivals, which in turn alter glitch onset, duration, and propagation. We introduce three metrics to determine whether a glitch can reveal sensitive value-dependent behavior: (1) change of glitch behavior across sensitive equivalence classes, (2) variation of glitch timing with the sensitive value, and (3) recurrence of glitches on the same internal node for one sensitive value but not another. Using these metrics, we show that timing perturbations can induce reproducible, sensitive-value-dependent glitches that indicate potential vulnerabilities. We support these observations with HSPICE supply-current NICV and correlation analyses, as well as post-route glitch-only NICV. We further complement the simulation study with the first-of-its-kind post-silicon optical probing measurements that support the same timing-difference mechanism in secure gadgets. Overall, our results show that even gadgets with formal probing security and composability guarantees can exhibit observable, data-dependent glitch patterns, motivating timing-aware refinement layers for secure hardware evaluation.

item.title: De-Folklorizing Paillier-Based VOLE: UC Security and Reusable Keys
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3029
Authors: Yehuda Lindell, Gil Segev
Summary: Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation (VOLE) is a fundamental building block underlying secure computation protocols. Protocols for threshold ECDSA and related applications commonly employ "folkloric" or implicit OLE-like constructions based on Paillier encryption. Although these embedded techniques are used to secure substantial value in the blockchain ecosystem, they lack standalone, context-independent security proofs, preventing their principled use as general-purpose composable building blocks. The practical risk of relying on such components without standalone analyses is illustrated by key-extraction vulnerabilities discovered in more than ten deployed wallets and libraries.
In this work, we "de-folklorize" this common approach. We present a two-message Paillier-based VOLE protocol that achieves two central goals:
-- We prove its security within the UC framework based on standard cryptographic assumptions. Although the core of Paillier-based OLE follows readily from additive homomorphism, obtaining a standalone UC-secure realization requires resolving nontrivial challenges arising from maliciously generated long-lived keys, the mismatch between Paillier plaintext arithmetic and VOLE's field arithmetic, and the concurrent reuse of shared setup state.
-- We address a critical deployment challenge by introducing explicit support for key reusability. We separate the protocol and its ideal functionality into an initialization phase and a subsequent repeatable execution phase. A single Paillier key can then be securely reused across any polynomial number of concurrent executions and across multiple clients, each of which receives and verifies a one-message, client-specific setup. Consequently, a server supporting $M$ clients maintains just one persistent Paillier secret-key state.
Finally, we validate our protocol through an experimental evaluation. Although our protocol has lower computational throughput than the state-of-the-art OT-based approach, it remains bandwidth-competitive and offers a significant deployment advantage: whereas the OT-based approach requires pairwise initialization and management of $M$ independent dynamic states for $M$ clients, our protocol requires only one persistent server key state, substantially simplifying state management in modern client-server architectures.

item.title: Improving Lindell's Two-Party ECDSA: Faster Key Generation and UC Security Without Global Abort
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3028
Authors: Yehuda Lindell, Gil Segev
Summary: The two-party ECDSA signing protocol constructed by Lindell (CRYPTO '17) has a substantial implementation footprint across the blockchain industry. Despite its advantage of completely static state management, the protocol admits two main limitations: (1) its key generation phase is computationally intensive due to the usage of somewhat inefficient zero-knowledge proofs, and (2) its security relies on a "global abort" mechanism (requiring that if a certain error is detected then all current and future executions must halt), which poses significant operational challenges in high-throughput environments.
In this work we demonstrate that these limitations are not inherent, presenting "drop-in" improvements that preserve the protocol's structure while delivering substantial gains in both efficiency and security:
-- Faster key generation. We overcome the main bottleneck in the protocol's key generation by constructing a drastically improved zero-knowledge proof for the Paillier-EC discrete logarithm (PDL) relation. Utilizing aggregated inner-product arguments (Bulletproofs), we address the algebraic mismatch between Paillier encryption and elliptic curves by constructing a "commitment bridge" that links a Paillier ciphertext to a set of Pedersen commitments over an elliptic curve. This allows us to minimize Paillier operations by shifting the computational cost to significantly faster elliptic-curve operations.
-- UC security without global abort. We augment the protocol with a highly efficient non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (integrated into the protocol's second message). We prove that this addition eliminates the need for a global abort mechanism, upgrading the protocol's security from its original game-based definition to UC security against malicious adversaries (under the Paillier and Strong RSA assumptions in the random oracle model).
We provide rigorous security proofs and report on the performance of a production-grade implementation, demonstrating that our approach reduces the estimated key-generation time by a factor of approximately four and achieves UC security without global abort with minimal signing overhead: less than $22$ms of additional computation per party and only $3.5$KB of additional communication.

item.title: Adams Bridge is Falling Down: A New Chosen Ciphertext Side-Channel Attack on the PQC Accelerator
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3027
Authors: Ruize Wang, Aikata, Péter Horváth, Thomas Szymkowiak, Markku-Juhani Saarinen, Lejla Batina
Summary: With ML-KEM and ML-DSA now standardized by NIST, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is moving from research into real world. Adams Bridge is an industry-oriented hardware accelerator that implements both ML-KEM and ML-DSA in a unified architecture. It is used as the post-quantum engine of Caliptra 2.1, a silicon root of trust designed to be integrated into data center chips from multiple vendors. This broad integration makes its security particularly important, as vulnerabilities could affect a wide range of deployed systems. In this paper, we reveal new vulnerabilities in the centered binomial sampling and ciphertext compression and comparison operations. We demonstrate the first practical key recovery attack on the released Adams Bridge v2.0.3 hardware implementation of ML-KEM with all countermeasures enabled. We further propose a new non-profiled chosen ciphertext attack method, achieving full secret key recovery for ML-KEM-1024 using 18 580 traces in 49.5 minutes. Compared to our profiled attack, the new method reduces the number of traces by at least 29.2%. More broadly, our findings highlight a gap between the countermeasures recommended by the research community and those adopted in industrial PQC hardware designs. As the transition to PQC accelerates, bridging this gap is crucial to ensuring the security of real-world deployments.

item.title: Minimizing Toffoli Gate Counts in In-Place S-Box Implementations
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3026
Authors: Seungjun Baek, Wonwoo Song, Namil Kim, Anubhab Baksi, Jongsung Kim
Summary: In this paper, we study ancilla-free in-place quantum implementations of the Ascon S-box and the 5-bit Keccak $\chi_5$ mapping. We develop a complete synthesis method that treats NOT and CNOT gates as affine operations and uses canonical state representation together with a proven lower bound to prune the search space. Using this method, we settle the previously unresolved minimum Toffoli count for the Ascon S-box at exactly seven, extend the same minimum to Keccak $\chi_5$ via affine equivalence, and establish a minimum Toffoli depth of seven for both functions. We further optimize Clifford+$T$ realizations of these minimum-Toffoli circuits by resynthesizing the decomposed circuits across Toffoli-decomposition boundaries. For both targets, the resulting implementations achieve either 33 $T$ gates with $T$-depth 8 or 29 $T$ gates with $T$-depth 10. To the best of our knowledge, these achieve the lowest reported $T$-depth and $T$-count, respectively, among existing 5-qubit ancilla-free in-place implementations.

item.title: EpochPIR: Low Amortized Communication PIR at Near-Optimal Throughput
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3025
Authors: Rasoul Akhavan Mahdavi, Sarvar Patel, Joon Young Seo, Kevin Yeo
Summary: Existing single-server private information retrieval (PIR) schemes face a sharp trade-off between server throughput and communication. Schemes built on SimplePIR scan the database at nearly memory bandwidth using native integer arithmetic, but require either a large client-side hint or hundreds of kilobytes of communication per query. Conversely, schemes based on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), such as Spiral, require only a few to tens of kilobytes per query, but process the database several times more slowly.
We present EpochPIR, a single-server PIR scheme that achieves amortized communication comparable to Spiral’s while maintaining server throughput close to SimplePIR’s. Our starting point is the observation that SimplePIR queries do not require independent secrets: under a fixed public matrix, the d negacyclic rotations of a single ring-LWE (RLWE) secret can safely serve as the secrets for d consecutive queries under the standard RLWE assumption. Uploading a single encrypted secret once every d queries allows the server to precompute the homomorphic hint-products for the entire batch of d queries, eliminating the per-query homomorphic hint evaluation of prior hintless schemes. Because the rotated secrets form a negacyclic Toeplitz matrix, the server can evaluate all d encrypted hint-products simultaneously in quasilinear time using two-dimensional number-theoretic transforms, producing the results directly in packed RLWE ciphertexts. This yields a modular two-stage framework: a SimplePIR-based column selector reduces PIR over the entire database to homomorphic selection over a single encrypted column, and any FHE row selector using long-lived client evaluation keys can then compress that column into a compact response with minimal impact on overall throughput.
Instantiated with a Spiral-style CMUX row selector, EpochPIR retrieves a 256-byte entry from an 8 GB database with 74 KB of communication per query at a sustained single-core throughput of 10.7 GB/s, 77% of SimplePIR’s, without a clientside hint. A communication-optimized variant communicates only 26 KB per query, 41× less than the hintless ReinsPIRe at 97% of its throughput and 25% less than Spiral at 14× its throughput.

item.title: CRAFTing an Attack on the Full-Round CRAFT
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3024
Authors: Orr Dunkelman, Eran Lambooij
Summary: CRAFT is a 64-bit block, 128-bit key tweakable block cipher presented in 2019 by Beierle et al. can be efficiently protected against differential fault attacks. Since its introduction, numerous attacks were presented, where the best one (in number of attacked rounds) can break up to 26 rounds out of the cipher's 32.
In this paper, we present the first full-round attack on CRAFT in the single-key model. The attack uses the recently presented (FSE 2026) observation that CRAFT can be decomposed into two parts, with minimal inter-part mixing. We use this property to construct a dissection attack that breaks the full 32-round CRAFT in $2^{121}$ time and $2^{120}$ memory, using 3 known plaintexts; an information-theoretic argument suggests that two already suffice. The same attack extends to 36 rounds of CRAFT in $2^{126}$ time and $2^{124}$ memory with 3 known plaintexts, and so remains faster than exhaustive search well beyond the specified number of rounds.

item.title: Beskar: Efficient Threshold ML-DSA via Preprocessed Rejection Sampling
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3023
Authors: Sebastian Kolby, Claudio Orlandi, Stanislas Pawlak
Summary: Efficient threshold variants of ML-DSA are important for the transition to post-quantum cryptography, as they allow parties to jointly produce standard ML-DSA signatures without reconstructing the signing key. The main obstacle is rejection sampling: before releasing a candidate signature, the parties must jointly evaluate several norm checks on secret-shared values and restart the computation if any check fails. In existing MPC-based protocols, these checks account for much of the cost of the online phase.
We present Beskar, a threshold ML-DSA protocol secure against malicious adversaries in the honest-majority setting. Building on Quorus (Bienstock et al., USENIX 2026), we reduce online signing from sixteen rounds to three and reduce online communication by a factor of 10. Our main technical contribution is a method for moving most of the computation required by rejection sampling into preprocessing and combining the remaining checks with signature release. In contrast to Mithril (Celi et al., USENIX 2026), Beskar relies only on standard secret sharing, rather than short secret sharing, and its expected number of signing attempts does not grow with the number of parties. Our implementation demonstrates practicality with a 5 party threshold signing attempt running in under 700ms in a high latency setting.

item.title: Automated Verification of Glitch- and Transition-Robust Composable Masked Circuits via Logic Simulations
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3022
Authors: Nicolai Müller, Amir Moradi
